paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose a portfolio with a strong Sharpe ratio while holding no more than m assets. This restriction matters because managing fewer active investments can reduce managerial and financial costs. It also makes optimization difficult: the method must determine which assets to include while optimizing a risk-adjusted return expressed as a ratio.

The authors transform this fractional optimization problem into an equivalent quadratic programming problem that preserves the asset-count constraint. This equivalence provides a different mathematical route to the same objective. They then use structural properties of the transformed objective, including the Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz property, to develop a proximal gradient algorithm and analyze its convergence rates.

Under certain conditions, the resulting portfolio attains the globally optimal Sharpe ratio among portfolios satisfying the sparsity constraint. The conditional nature of this guarantee matters: the abstract does not claim global optimality for every possible instance. The contribution is a theoretically supported route to optimizing both portfolio sparsity and risk-adjusted return together.
neurips-2024-a-globally-optimal-portfoli.tldr: An equivalent quadratic formulation enables a proximal gradient method with conditional global-optimality guarantees for Sharpe-ratio portfolios holding at most m assets.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using data collected under a different policy. This is valuable when directly testing a new policy is difficult. Existing estimators can face a tradeoff between unstable predictions caused by high variance and systematic errors that remain even as more data become available.

The paper introduces STAR, a framework that simplifies complex state spaces into compact, discrete models called abstract reward processes. These abstractions let the framework work with problems whose original states may be continuous. STAR encompasses multiple estimators, including existing approaches as special cases, rather than prescribing a single estimation procedure.

The authors prove that predictions from abstract reward processes estimated using off-policy data are consistent, meaning they become correct asymptotically. Their experiments also examine practical prediction error: the best STAR estimator beats the baselines in all twelve studied cases, while the median STAR estimator does so in seven. These findings support the framework's usefulness while distinguishing its long-run correctness guarantee from its observed finite-data performance.
neurips-2024-abstract-reward-processes-l.tldr: STAR uses compact state abstractions to support consistent off-policy evaluation and empirically reduce prediction error.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation aims to represent a large training dataset with a much smaller collection of synthesized examples. But reducing the images does not necessarily reduce all storage costs. The paper reports that, in ImageNet condensation, auxiliary soft labels can require more than thirty times as much storage as the condensed dataset itself.

The authors connect this burden to a lack of diversity among synthesized images belonging to the same class. They attribute that similarity to earlier methods combining different classes within a batch for batch-normalization matching. Their approach instead groups samples within each class during image synthesis, introducing class-wise supervision that increases within-class diversity.

With more diverse images, the required soft labels can be compressed through simple random pruning rather than complex pruning rules. In the reported ImageNet-1K setting with 200 images per class, label storage falls from 113 GB to 2.8 GB, alongside a reported 2.6% performance gain. The result shows that improving the condensed images themselves can substantially reduce the supporting label storage.
neurips-2024-are-large-scale-soft-labels.tldr: Class-wise image synthesis increases condensed-data diversity, enabling much smaller soft-label storage through random pruning.

paragraphs: Language-model benchmarks become less informative when models master their questions or encounter benchmark content through leakage. Creating replacement datasets by hand is costly. This paper investigates whether existing benchmarks can instead be updated automatically while maintaining useful difficulty levels and stable evaluation behavior.

The authors propose two strategies. Mimicking generates new examples that resemble the originals in style and context. Extending expands existing examples across different cognitive levels using Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives. Together, these strategies provide ways to refresh familiar benchmark material and adjust how demanding the resulting questions are.

Experiments with updated MMLU and BIG-Bench support the stability of the strategies. Mimicking alleviates performance overestimation associated with benchmark leakage, and extending shows promise in cases where mimicking fails. Difficulty control also helps distinguish model capabilities more finely: an evaluation can reveal little when its questions are overwhelmingly easy or hard. The findings support automated updating as a practical evaluation approach, without establishing that every generated update eliminates leakage or produces an equally informative test.
neurips-2024-automating-dataset-updates-.tldr: Automatically mimicking and extending benchmark questions can refresh evaluations, reduce leakage-related overestimation, and control difficulty.

paragraphs: Preference-learning systems often ask people to choose between two options. These binary answers identify a preferred option but provide limited information about how strongly it is preferred. The paper investigates response time as an additional signal, drawing on its inverse relationship with preference strength.

The authors develop a computationally efficient estimator that combines choices with response times to infer human utility functions. Its foundation is the EZ diffusion model from psychology. Their theoretical and empirical analyses show that response times are particularly informative for queries involving strong preferences, where the timing adds information beyond the choice itself.

The estimator is then incorporated into preference-based linear bandits for identifying the best option within a fixed budget. Simulations using three real-world datasets show faster preference learning than approaches using choices alone. The contribution is therefore both an estimation method and its integration into an interactive learning procedure. The stated findings concern gains from an additional behavioral signal, especially in strong-preference queries, rather than a claim that every individual response time perfectly measures preference.
neurips-2024-enhancing-preference-based-.tldr: Combining human choices with response times improves utility estimation and accelerates preference learning in the studied settings.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a model use examples in a prompt to perform a task without changing its parameters. Many explanations of this ability assume training examples already organized like the eventual task. This paper instead asks how such abilities can emerge from unstructured text and which properties of the data and model make that possible.

The authors show that co-occurrence between semantically related word pairs can support several in-context learning capabilities. In particular, they prove that word-analogy completion can arise through co-occurrence modeling in a continuous bag-of-words model. For that result, neither attention mechanisms nor positional information is required, making the source of the capability simpler than those architectural features.

Other tasks have different requirements. Positional information becomes crucial for the studied logical reasoning tasks that generalize to unseen tokens. The authors also identify failures when reasoning requires unseen patterns and when analogy-related pairs occur only at fixed training positions. These distinctions show why successful in-context learning on one kind of task does not establish the same generalization ability on another.
neurips-2024-from-unstructured-data-to-i.tldr: The paper connects in-context learning from unstructured text to co-occurrence and positional structure, identifying both sufficient mechanisms and failure cases.

paragraphs: Language models require substantial amounts of text, but available corpora tend to provide sufficient coverage mainly for languages with large, dominant communities. This paper addresses a resource gap for minority languages. It focuses on combining broad language coverage, reproducible collection, and rigorous cleaning in a single openly available corpus.

The resulting resource, GlotCC, contains 2 TB of general-domain text derived from CommonCrawl and covers more than 1,000 languages. It is organized at the document level. The authors present it as a cleaned corpus, addressing the noise that can make large web-derived collections difficult to trust for research use.

The release includes both the text collection and the system that produced it: the processing pipeline, language-identification model, and filters. Providing these components makes the construction process available for inspection and reproduction, alongside the finished data. The contribution is therefore broader than assembling multilingual text. It supplies an open method for producing a corpus with wide language coverage and makes minority-language data more accessible to the research community.
neurips-2024-glotcc-an-open-broad-covera.tldr: GlotCC releases a cleaned 2 TB web-text corpus covering over 1,000 languages together with its reproducible processing pipeline.

paragraphs: The paper studies sparse regression when linear measurements are distributed across a network of agents. A sparse model uses relatively few active parameters. Existing decentralized approaches commonly encourage sparsity through an explicit LASSO penalty; this work investigates whether the optimization process itself can produce an appropriately sparse solution.

The authors apply decentralized gradient descent to an over-parameterized, nonconvex least-squares formulation without a penalty. With good network connectivity, small initialization, and early stopping, they show that the method can reach statistically optimal accuracy. They also give sufficient conditions governing initialization, step size, connectivity, and stopping time, and recover the centralized gradient-descent convergence rate.

Building on this analysis, they introduce T-DGD, which truncates iterates before agents transmit them. In the high signal-to-noise regime, T-DGD achieves accuracy comparable to ordinary decentralized gradient descent while making communication cost logarithmic in the number of parameters. Numerical results support both methods. The guarantees tie the benefits of implicit regularization and reduced communication to specific optimization, network, and signal conditions.
neurips-2024-implicit-regularization-of-.tldr: Under sufficient conditions, decentralized gradient descent learns sparse models without explicit penalties, with a truncated variant reducing communication at high signal-to-noise ratios.

paragraphs: Experiments intended to intervene on a causal system do not always produce data from the intended intervention alone. Their observations may mix intended interventions, unintended interventions, and observational behavior. The paper asks whether these components can be disentangled even when the underlying causal graph is unknown.

The analysis considers linear structural equation models with Gaussian additive noise. Within this setting, the authors show that both do interventions and soft interventions produce distributions with enough diversity and suitable properties to recover the mixture components efficiently. They also relate the number of samples required to the magnitude of the intervention's change to the affected variables' governing equations: larger changes make disentangling easier.

After separating the mixture, the causal graph can be identified up to its interventional Markov equivalence class. This matches the stated level of identification available when intervention generation is not contaminated by mixing; it does not necessarily identify one unique graph. Simulations of causal discovery from mixed data support the theoretical analysis, linking recovery of the intervention components to recovery of causal structure.
neurips-2024-learning-mixtures-of-unknow.tldr: For linear Gaussian causal models, intervention-induced distribution differences enable recovery of mixed data components and causal identification up to an equivalence class.

paragraphs: Graphical models describe systems in which variables depend on one another, making uncertainty estimation more complicated than treating each prediction independently. The paper describes a tradeoff in existing methods: sampling-based approaches can be slow and lack convergence guarantees, while faster closed-form alternatives can underestimate uncertainty.

LinUProp changes how uncertainty moves between related nodes. It combines their uncertainty additively rather than multiplicatively, yielding a method with linear scalability, closed-form solutions, and guaranteed convergence without the stated underestimation problem. The authors also decompose expected prediction error and prove that LinUProp computes the generalized variance component of that decomposition, giving its uncertainty estimate a defined mathematical interpretation.

Experiments show agreement with the sampling-based method while retaining fast convergence and linear scalability. The authors further test whether these estimates help decide which examples to label in active learning. Across four real-world graph datasets, LinUProp achieves higher accuracy with a smaller labeling budget than competing methods. This connects the uncertainty calculation to a concrete decision benefit beyond computational efficiency alone.
neurips-2024-linear-uncertainty-quantifi.tldr: LinUProp propagates uncertainty additively across graphs, combining theoretical guarantees with efficient estimation and improved active-learning results.

paragraphs: Long input sequences can make language-model inference expensive because self-attention requires substantial computation and memory access. Loki tackles this cost by examining the key vectors used inside attention. The authors find that these vectors occupy a substantially lower-dimensional space, an observation that holds consistently across several evaluated models and datasets.

The method uses that lower-dimensional representation to calculate attention scores for ranking and selecting tokens from the key-value cache. This provides a cheaper way to decide which cached tokens deserve attention. The low-dimensional calculation is therefore central to token selection, connecting a structural observation about the vectors to a sparse attention procedure.

In the reported evaluations, Loki accelerates attention by reducing both computation and the movement of data through load and store operations. It also preserves model effectiveness better than the popular approximation methods included in those evaluations. The result supports exploiting the observed geometry of key vectors to make attention more efficient, with the stated evidence applying across the tested models and datasets.
neurips-2024-loki-low-rank-keys-for-effi.tldr: Loki uses low-dimensional key representations to select cached tokens cheaply, speeding attention while preserving model effectiveness in evaluations.

paragraphs: Training models to generate long videos requires examples that capture events over time. Short clips provide a different kind of training material, and high-quality long videos are scarce. This paper targets videos that last at least ten seconds, contain no cuts, show substantial motion and varied content, and include detailed captions across time.

The authors build a pipeline that filters source videos using quantitative assessments of scene cuts, motion, and semantic content. A hierarchical captioning procedure then supplies temporally dense descriptions for the selected videos. The two stages address complementary needs: choosing suitable continuous footage and describing what happens throughout it.

The resulting LVD-2M dataset contains two million long-take videos, each longer than ten seconds and paired with temporally dense captions. The authors assess its usefulness by fine-tuning video-generation models to produce longer videos with dynamic motion. This supports the dataset's intended role as training material for long-video generation, while the claim that it will substantially advance future research remains the authors' expectation.
neurips-2024-lvd-2m-a-long-take-video-da.tldr: LVD-2M provides two million continuous videos longer than ten seconds, with dense temporal captions for long-video generation research.

paragraphs: Generated code can produce the right answer yet take unnecessarily long to run. Mercury evaluates this distinction, addressing benchmarks that mainly reward functional correctness. It contains 1,889 Python tasks with accompanying solutions that provide efficiency baselines and allow the authors to examine distributions of execution time.

The paper introduces Beyond, a score that weights passing solutions according to their runtime percentile. This combines correctness and computational efficiency in one measurement. Ideally, Beyond would align with the ordinary Pass score; a gap between them indicates that some functionally correct outputs fall short on efficiency.

On Mercury, leading code models reach 65% on Pass but remain below 50% on Beyond, exposing an efficiency gap that correctness alone would obscure. The authors also compare training approaches and find that Direct Preference Optimization provides a robust baseline for improving efficiency relative to supervised fine-tuning in their experiments. The benchmark thus supplies both a way to measure efficient code generation and empirical evidence for a promising improvement strategy.
neurips-2024-mercury-a-code-efficiency-b.tldr: Mercury evaluates correctness and runtime together, revealing efficiency gaps in generated Python code and promising results from preference optimization.

paragraphs: NaturalBench examines whether vision-language models actually use images to answer questions that humans find easy. Its natural adversarial samples come from ordinary image-text collections, assembled through a semi-automated process using existing models and human verification. The benchmark contains 10,000 verified visual-question-answering samples.

Its central design pairs each question with two images requiring different answers. A model cannot answer both correctly merely by relying on the question's wording or common knowledge. Each sample also receives between one and eight skill tags, allowing analysis of overlapping demands such as attribute binding, object relationships, logic, and counting.

Across 53 evaluated models, the authors report a substantial gap behind human performance, which exceeds 90%. They also find models often repeat an answer despite changes in the image, exposing biases that debiasing can help address. Applying the collection method to long captions and to Chinese and Hindi data demonstrates its potential for broader, changing evaluations. The findings connect poor performance to both combined reasoning demands and insufficient sensitivity to visual evidence.
neurips-2024-naturalbench-evaluating-vis.tldr: NaturalBench pairs questions with images requiring different answers, exposing large human-model gaps and visual insensitivity across 53 models.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes how quickly BFGS converges when step sizes are chosen through an inexact line search satisfying the Armijo-Wolfe conditions. Its contribution is explicit, non-asymptotic global rates: bounds that characterize progress over iterations rather than describing only eventual behavior close to a solution.

For strongly convex objectives with Lipschitz gradients, the authors establish a linear rate of (1 − 1/κ)^t, where κ is the ratio of gradient smoothness to strong convexity. With a Lipschitz Hessian, they also obtain a linear rate depending only on line-search parameters, independent of that condition number. The analysis additionally establishes a global superlinear rate of order (1/t)^t.

The global bounds permit any starting point and any symmetric positive definite initial Hessian approximation. However, the initial approximation influences how many iterations are needed to achieve the stated rates. The authors combine these results into a global complexity characterization and specify a step-size selection mechanism satisfying the line-search conditions, including its overall complexity. This links convergence theory to the actual procedure for choosing steps.
neurips-2024-non-asymptotic-global-conve.tldr: The paper establishes explicit global convergence and complexity bounds for BFGS with Armijo-Wolfe line search under stated convexity and smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization in Wasserstein space, where the objects being optimized are probability distributions. It considers objectives that are nonconvex along generalized geodesics, the paths used in the analysis of this space. The central question is how to obtain convergence results when the objective lacks convexity along these paths.

The authors focus on objectives with a difference-of-convex structure along generalized geodesics. This means the nonconvexity retains a particular mathematical organization that the algorithm can exploit. Their framework also includes sampling problems whose target distribution has a logarithm with difference-of-convex structure, connecting the optimization setting to the task of generating samples.

They introduce a semi Forward-Backward Euler scheme and derive convergence insights across several nonconvex regimes, including potentially nonsmooth ones. The scheme is only a slight modification of Forward-Backward Euler. According to the authors, convergence of the latter remains unknown in their very general setting. The significance is that this small algorithmic change permits convergence analysis for structured problems beyond the geodesically convex case.
neurips-2024-non-geodesically-convex-opt.tldr: A modified Forward-Backward Euler scheme yields convergence insights for structured nonconvex optimization over probability distributions.

paragraphs: In-context learning depends on examples placed in a model's prompt. Although earlier work reported robustness to noisy demonstrations in classification, this paper finds that noisy annotations substantially harm text-generation tasks. The distinction matters because selecting relevant examples does not ensure that their inputs and labels actually match.

The authors introduce Local Perplexity Ranking, or LPR, to replace suspect candidate demonstrations with nearby examples that are more likely to be clean. Their motivation comes from separating perplexity into an inherent component and a matching component. Ranking within semantic neighborhoods helps isolate the signal associated with input-label compatibility rather than relying on an undifferentiated perplexity score.

The approach aims to prevent mismatched pairs from entering the prompt while preserving the usefulness of the original demonstration-selection method. Experiments on common benchmarks with noisy annotations show exact-match score improvements of up to 18.75. That figure is the largest reported improvement, not a uniform gain across tasks. The findings show that local checking of candidate demonstrations can improve generation when the example pool contains annotation noise.
neurips-2024-on-the-noise-robustness-of-.tldr: Local Perplexity Ranking replaces suspect demonstrations with cleaner semantic neighbors, improving text-generation performance under annotation noise.

paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent supports distributed training when workers have different computing speeds. Momentum is useful in deep-model training, but previous work has found that adding it naively to asynchronous updates can interfere with convergence. This paper addresses how to incorporate momentum while accounting for the ordering of gradients.

The proposed method, ordered momentum or OrMo, organizes gradients according to their iteration indices when incorporating momentum into asynchronous SGD. The authors prove convergence for nonconvex problems with both constant learning rates and learning rates that adapt to delay. Their analysis does not depend on the maximum delay, which they identify as a first for convergence analysis of asynchronous SGD with momentum.

Experiments show better convergence performance than ordinary asynchronous SGD and other evaluated asynchronous momentum methods. The theoretical and empirical results support the importance of how gradients are ordered when momentum is accumulated. The absence of maximum-delay dependence is a property of the stated convergence analysis; the abstract does not claim that all aspects of training performance are unaffected by delays.
neurips-2024-ordered-momentum-for-asynch.tldr: OrMo orders gradients by iteration index to integrate momentum into asynchronous SGD, with convergence analysis independent of maximum delay.

paragraphs: In partially observable environments, an agent needs representations that retain information beyond its current observation. Recurrent neural networks can provide this memory. For agents learning continuously during interaction, real-time recurrent learning is an attractive training approach, but its computational cost is prohibitive for standard recurrent architectures.

The paper builds on linear recurrent architectures, which replace dense recurrent weights with a complex-valued diagonal structure. That architectural change makes real-time recurrent learning efficient. The authors introduce Recurrent Trace Units, a small modification of these architectures intended to provide a lightweight and effective recurrent model for online reinforcement learning.

Despite the modest architectural change, the authors find substantial performance benefits over linear recurrent units when both are trained with real-time recurrent learning. Across several partially observable environments, Recurrent Trace Units also significantly outperform GRUs and Transformers while requiring substantially less computation. These results support designing the recurrent architecture around efficient online training, with the reported advantage established in the environments evaluated rather than as a universal ranking of sequence models.
neurips-2024-real-time-recurrent-learnin.tldr: Recurrent Trace Units enable efficient online recurrent learning and outperform evaluated alternatives in several partially observable reinforcement-learning environments.

paragraphs: SafeSora is a dataset for studying how text-to-video generation can better reflect human preferences and reduce harmful outputs. It treats helpfulness and harmlessness as separate dimensions of evaluation. This provides a structured basis for studying both whether a generated video serves the request and whether its content is acceptable to human annotators.

The annotation design breaks helpfulness into four sub-dimensions and harmlessness into twelve sub-categories, which guide pilot annotations and crowdworker reasoning. The dataset contains 14,711 unique prompts, 57,333 unique videos generated by four models, and 51,691 pairs of human preference annotations. These comparisons provide training and evaluation material for preference-based alignment research.

The authors demonstrate applications that include training a text-video moderation model and aligning generation by fine-tuning either a prompt augmentation module or the diffusion model. These examples establish uses for the dataset at different points in the generation process. They support SafeSora's potential as a foundation for preference modeling and alignment-method development, rather than establishing that models trained with it are universally harmless.
neurips-2024-safesora-towards-safety-ali.tldr: SafeSora supplies structured human preferences over generated videos and demonstrates applications in moderation and text-to-video alignment.

paragraphs: Large language models may exceed consumer GPU memory, requiring parameters to be offloaded to RAM or SSD. Under parameter offloading, processing hundreds or thousands of tokens in a batch can take about as long as processing one. SpecExec is designed to exploit that execution pattern for faster generation on consumer machines.

A draft model proposes likely continuations, which SpecExec organizes into a tree serving as a cache for the target model. The target model validates that tree in a single pass. This parallel checking lets a target-model iteration contribute multiple generated tokens; the authors report up to twenty tokens per iteration for popular model families.

With RAM offloading on consumer GPUs, the authors demonstrate inference for models exceeding 50 billion parameters at four to six tokens per second using 4-bit quantization, or two to three using 16-bit weights. These results illustrate how the hardware setting changes the useful decoding strategy: large parallel batches can make expensive target-model passes produce more output in the tested offloading configurations.
neurips-2024-specexec-massively-parallel.tldr: SpecExec validates trees of drafted continuations in parallel to accelerate large-model generation with parameter offloading on consumer GPUs.

paragraphs: Selecting the top k items is a recurring operation in deep learning, and the cost of ranking can become significant. This paper proposes ST_k, a fully differentiable module with a single trainable parameter. The authors design it to solve top-k problems without requiring additional time or GPU memory.

Full differentiability allows the selection module to participate in end-to-end optimization within a neural network's computational graph. The authors apply it to Average Top-k Loss, an objective that itself requires top-k selection. This produces ST_k Loss, connecting the proposed selection mechanism directly to the loss used for model training.

Across multiple benchmarks, ST_k Loss outperforms Average Top-k Loss and achieves the best reported average performance with the lowest standard deviation. The authors also report surpassing the state of the art on the CIFAR-100-LT and Places-LT leaderboards using this loss. These findings support the module's value through its demonstrated loss-function application, while its differentiable design makes integration into a unified training computation possible.
neurips-2024-st-k-a-scalable-module-for-.tldr: ST_k makes top-k selection differentiable with one trainable parameter and improves benchmark performance when incorporated into a training loss.

paragraphs: The secretary problem studies online selection when items arrive in random order and decisions must be made as they appear. Its classical competitive-ratio limit is 1/e, approximately 0.368. This paper asks how little advance information is enough to improve that guarantee, allowing for predictions that may be inaccurate.

The proposed information is an additive gap: the difference between the highest weight and the kth-highest weight. Item weights remain fixed by an adversary, and arrival order remains random. The algorithm receives the gap rather than detailed knowledge of the weights, and knowing this quantity exactly does not make selection trivial.

For any k and any gap, the authors establish a competitive ratio of 0.4 when the gap is exact, even when k itself is unknown. This exceeds the classical bound by a constant. A modified algorithm also provides robustness-consistency guarantees and improved guarantees when a range for prediction error is known. The result demonstrates the usefulness of this limited advice without establishing that it is the weakest possible information in every formulation.
neurips-2024-the-secretary-problem-with-.tldr: Knowing an exact gap between the largest and kth-largest weights enables a 0.4 competitive ratio, even without knowing k.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduces the amount of model customization that must be stored, but storage and transmission can still become substantial when serving many users or tasks. VB-LoRA targets these remaining costs by sharing the parameters used to construct low-rank adaptations across the model.

Its divide-and-share approach uses a global bank of vectors across matrix dimensions, modules, and layers. A differentiable top-k admixture module combines vectors from this bank to construct all the low-rank matrices used by LoRA. This allows different adaptation matrices to draw from shared parameters, reducing how much separate information must be stored.

Experiments cover natural-language understanding, generation, instruction tuning, and mathematical reasoning. The authors report comparable or better performance than state-of-the-art parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. In the stated Llama2-13B experiment, VB-LoRA uses only 0.4% of LoRA's stored parameters and achieves superior results. This percentage compares stored adaptation parameters with LoRA, not with the full language model. The findings support global parameter sharing as an effective way to compress task-specific customization.
neurips-2024-vb-lora-extreme-parameter-e.tldr: VB-LoRA constructs adaptation matrices from a shared vector bank, sharply reducing stored parameters while maintaining strong evaluated performance.

paragraphs: Zero-shot reinforcement learning aims to prepare an agent for tasks after an offline pre-training phase that uses no rewards. Methods based on successor measures and successor features have performed well, but they depend on large, varied pre-training datasets. This paper examines what happens when only small, homogeneous datasets are available.

The authors investigate the resulting performance degradation and propose changes inspired by conservatism in single-task offline reinforcement learning. Their goal is to improve zero-shot learning under restricted data coverage. They evaluate these conservative approaches across multiple datasets, domains, and tasks, allowing comparison under both low-quality and high-quality data conditions.

In the reported evaluations, conservative methods outperform their non-conservative counterparts on low-quality datasets and perform no worse on high-quality ones. They also outperform evaluated baselines that receive task information during training. These are empirical findings across the studied settings, rather than a guarantee of success on every future task. The results suggest that ideas developed for single-task offline learning can help make zero-shot preparation useful with less diverse data.
neurips-2024-zero-shot-reinforcement-lea.tldr: Conservative zero-shot reinforcement-learning methods improve performance with small, homogeneous datasets without degrading results on the evaluated high-quality datasets.
